If your research involves participants reacting to linguistic stimuli
such as words, sentences, or vignettes,
there's a pretty simple way to make your articles and presentations
more informative: Also show the results aggregated by stimuli
rather than just by participants.
Regardless of whether or not you're fitting mixed-effects models incorporating
random effects for stimuli, such by-stimulus visualisations may help both
you and your readership identify patterns in the data that a by-participant
visualisation would gloss over and guard against premature conclusions.


## Examples

As a simple first example, consider a small-scale study by Kuster (2018),
in which the student-author sought to replicate a study by Laufer (2000) 
in a different setting.
Ten English-speaking learners of L2 German were given twenty fill-in-the-blank
sentences that targeted German idioms.
Following Laufer (2000), the idioms were separated into four categories:

1. German idioms for which Kuster (2018) could not identify a corresponding
English idiom (e.g., _sich aus dem Staub machen_ 'to make off');
2. German idioms for which Kuster found a corresponding English idiom
with no formal overlap to the German idiom (e.g., _Ich verstehe nur Bahnhof_ 'It's all Greek to me'; 
literally 'I only understand railway station').
This category is referred to as _only conceptual overlap_;
3. German idioms with a formally somewhat similar English counterpart
(e.g., _Katzen hageln_ 'to rain cats and dogs').
This category is referred to as _partial formal overlap_;
4. German idioms with a formally very similar English counterpart,
that is, the German and English idioms are essentially literal translations of one another
(e.g., _zwischen den Zeilen lesen_ 'to read between the lines').
This category is referred to as _total formal overlap_.

The expectation was that the learners would tend to give more 
idiom responses to the higher-numbered categories than to the lower-numbered ones.
The results in @fig-boxplot-kuster are in line with these expectations.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![The boxplots with individual data points overlaid show the differences between the participants for each idiom category.](index_files/figure-html/fig-boxplot-kuster-1.svg){#fig-boxplot-kuster width=80%}
:::
:::


The boxplots with the individual participants' results overlaid 
are already [much better](../2016-06-21-drawing-a-boxplot/#adding-the-individual-data-points)
than a typical bar chart that only shows the mean proportion for each
idiom category.
My suggestion, though, is to _also_ show the variability in the data
by idiom, as in @fig-dotplot-kuster.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![A Cleveland dotplot of the by-idiom results shows the variation within and the overlap between the categories.](index_files/figure-html/fig-dotplot-kuster-1.svg){#fig-dotplot-kuster width=80%}
:::
:::


This Cleveland dotplot has a few things going for it.

First, it illustrates the extent to which stimuli within a single category
differ in how frequently they elicit a certain response.
This, hopefully, helps guard against prematurely reifying fairly abstract
stimulus categories and their role in language learning.
In this example, the results for the _only conceptual overlap_ category
overlap with those for all other categories so that it's clear that we can
predict little about any future idiom we might assign to this category.

Second, stimulus labels, more often so than participant labels, carry meaning.
In Cleveland dotplots, we can include these labels.
Sometimes, these labels may help us or our readership to come up with reasonable
accounts for the by-stimulus variability.
Further, as in the present case, they highlight that the categories are to 
some extent arbitrary, and readers may call into question some classifications.
For instance, someone with sufficient German and English may look at @fig-dotplot-kuster 
and rightly wonder why _Kinderspiel_ 'child's play' is in the _only conceptual overlap_
category rather than in one of the _formal overlap_ categories.
The categorisation of some other idioms can similarly be questioned.

Third, readers who disagree with some categorisations can nonetheless gauge
if the overall results would change if the stimuli were to be categorised
differently.
In this example, assigning _Kinderspiel_ to one of the _formal overlap_
categories wouldn't affect the overall finding.




::: {.cell}

:::



::: {.cell}

:::


As a second example, consider an older study of mine (Vanhove 2017),
in which I asked a number of Dutch-speaking participants from the Netherlands (NL)
and Belgium (BE) to assign articles to German nouns with Dutch cognates.
@fig-boxplot-vanhove shows how often these participants assigned the neuter
article _das_ to four categories of nouns:

1. neuter German (Gm.) nouns with a neuter Standard Dutch (St. Du.) cognate (e.g., Gm. _Brot_ -- St. Du. _brood_ 'bread');
2. masculine or feminine German nouns with a neuter Standard Dutch cognate (e.g., _Strand_ 'beach', which is masculine in German but _obviously_ should be neuter);
3. neuter German nouns with a common Standard Dutch cognate[^1] (e.g., Gm. _Beil_ -- St. Du. _bijl_ 'axe'; another aberration of the German language);
4. masculine or feminine German nouns with a common Standard Dutch cognate (e.g., _Berg_ 'mountain').

[^1]: For all intents and purposes, Standard Dutch doesn't distinguish between masculine and feminine gender adnominally.
The merger of masculine and feminine gender resulted in a common (non-neuter) gender category.
Lots of Flemish dialects still do to some extent, though. 
In these dialects, the distinction between masculine and feminine genders is especially marked on the indefinite article (e.g., _ne voet_ 'a foot (m.)' but _een hand_ 'a hand (f.)').


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Boxplots show considerable differences between participants in their propensity to assign a neuter article to German nouns.](index_files/figure-html/fig-boxplot-vanhove-1.svg){#fig-boxplot-vanhove width=50%}
:::
:::


These boxplots are all right.
But I like the Cleveland dotplot in @fig-dotplot-vanhove much better because
the data points carry much more meaning.
First, it highlights that, on the word level, there is hardly any overlap
between nouns with neuter cognates and those with common cognates,
suggesting that Standard Dutch gender strongly influences these participants'
responses.
The sole exception to this pattern is easily identified to be _Boot_, 
for which one plausible explanation is the participants' familiarity with
the film _Das Boot_.
And in case anyone was wondering whether the tendency of people from Antwerp
to refer to Antwerp as _'t Stad_ 'the city', which could be superficially read
as considering _stad_ to be neuter rather than common[^2], has any consequences,
the dotplot shows that none of the participants assigned a neuter article
to its German cognate _Stadt_.

[^2]: In Standard Dutch, _'t_ is a reduced form of the neuter article _het_.
But in _'t stad_ it can best be understood as a misspelling of _d'_, which
would be a reduced form of the common article _de_ and which is affected by
anticipatory devoicing.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![A Cleveland dotplot of the data aggregated by noun shows that, by and large, Belgian and Dutch speakers of Dutch show the same tendencies and that, with a single exception, there is no overlap between nouns with neuter cognates and those with common cognates. The sole exception, _Boot_, is easily identified; a plausible explanation for this result is that many participants may have known the film _Das Boot_. ](index_files/figure-html/fig-dotplot-vanhove-1.svg){#fig-dotplot-vanhove width=75%}
:::
:::


## Tips

**Tip 1.** Cleveland dotplots tend to work well for results aggregated by stimuli
as you can put the stimuli themselves or some shorter form of them in the graph.
Don't use bar charts; they tend to be too busy.

**Tip 2.** When working with facets (e.g., for different stimulus categories),
impose some sensible ordering. For instance, you could sort the facets
by the average response on the stimuli occurring in it.

**Tip 3.** Similarly, impose some sensible ordering on the stimuli within
the facets.

**Tip 4.** Have the graph show the item labels horizontally rather than
vertically.
